Prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties if available.
Encourage neighbours to also scout their fields at the same time, particularly when
All farm implements need to be sterilised over fire or with bleach, especially when cutting cassava stems into planting materials (cuttings).
Intercrop cassava with maize, beans or sunflower as trap crops for the whiteflies, the main vector of the disease.
Uproot and bury all cassava volunteer plants.
Remove weeds to discourage habitats for the vectors.
Harvest early, don't leave tubers for more than 9 months in the soil as this increase the chances of getting the virus.
Monitoring: Sometimes symptoms only occur on tubers, not leaves, and sometimes they only occur on leaves, not tubers.
Symptoms may appear and disappear in young plants, but appear again in cassava plants at a later stage.
Leaves: patchy yellowing along the thin secondary veins which are more prominent on mature (bottom) leaves.
This can spread and form bigger patches, with a ‘feathery’ or ‘blotchy’ appearance.
Stems: brown streaks and spots on upper green portions and necrotic lesion on the leaf scar.
May show shoot top death which can progress into die-back.
Begin with localised dead areas that are yellow-brown, with a cork-like appearance, and characteristic white threads on the outside of the tuber.
Some tubers have restricted growth, appearing like a series of rings stuck together.
Occurs alongside cassava mosaic disease (CMD) which is also spread by whiteflies and in infected planting material but the symptoms differ.
Daily monitor for the presence of whiteflies and take action when one whitefly is seen.
Direct Control: Remove diseased plants and dry all stems to use them as fire wood or stakes for climbing crops like beans.
However symptomless plants may still contain the virus.
There are no chemicals against viruses.
